summary: Lynestrenol is a synthetic 19-nortestosterone-derived progestogen marketed outside the USA (for example as Exluton/Exlutena 0.5 mg and Orgametril 5 mg). It is a prodrug that is rapidly and almost completely converted in the liver to active norethisterone, which binds progesterone receptors. At 0.5 mg it is a progestogen-only minipill whose main contraceptive action is thickening of cervical mucus to reduce sperm penetration, plus endometrial changes that hinder implantation, with ovulation inhibited in roughly 70% of users. It does not appreciably affect carbohydrate or lipid metabolism or haemostasis and is suitable during breastfeeding. At 5 mg it is used for menstrual disorders, endometriosis, benign breast disease, and to postpone or suppress menstruation. The most common adverse effect is an altered bleeding pattern. It is contraindicated in pregnancy, active venous thromboembolism, active or severe liver disease, undiagnosed vaginal bleeding, and sex-steroid-sensitive malignancies. Lynestrenol is NOT FDA-approved and has never been marketed in the United States.

moa: Lynestrenol is a synthetic 19-norsteroid progestogen prodrug. After oral intake it undergoes rapid, almost complete first-pass conversion in the liver to active norethisterone, which binds progesterone receptors in target organs such as the myometrium and endometrium. Its contraceptive effect is primarily due to increased cervical-mucus viscosity that reduces sperm penetration, together with endometrial changes that hinder nidation; ovulation is inhibited in about 70% of women (more consistently at the 5 mg dose). It has no clinically significant effect on carbohydrate or lipid metabolism or on haemostasis.

preg: Lynestrenol is contraindicated in pregnancy and should be stopped immediately if pregnancy occurs. Epidemiological data on oral contraceptives have not shown a teratogenic signal.
lact: The low-dose (0.5 mg) progestogen-only pill is suitable during breastfeeding, with no effect on milk production or quality; only about 0.14% of the daily dose is excreted in milk and no adverse effects on infant growth or development have been reported. Data are insufficient for the 5 mg Orgametril strength, which some national labels contraindicate in lactation.
renal: No specific dose adjustment is given in the SmPC.
hepatic: Lynestrenol is contraindicated in active or severe liver disease, and should be used only after liver function tests have normalized; no specific dose is defined for milder impairment.

major: Hepatic enzyme inducers reduce contraceptive efficacy and may cause breakthrough bleeding - phenytoin, barbiturates, primidone, carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, topiramate, felbamate, rifampicin, rifabutin, ritonavir, nelfinavir, griseofulvin, and St. John's wort; use a barrier method during and for 28 days after stopping the inducer
moderate: May increase cyclosporine levels and decrease lamotrigine levels
Activated charcoal reduces absorption of the contraceptive tablet
minor: May affect laboratory tests of liver, thyroid, adrenal, and renal function, carrier proteins, and coagulation parameters
interactions.diagnostics: May alter the results of certain endocrine and liver function laboratory tests.

missed: Take the missed contraceptive tablet as soon as you remember and the next tablet at the usual time. If more than 27 hours have passed since the last tablet (more than 3 hours late), use a barrier method for the next 7 days; if a tablet was missed in the first week and intercourse occurred in the preceding 7 days, consider the possibility of pregnancy. Vomiting or severe diarrhoea within 3-4 hours counts as a missed tablet.
overdose: There are no reports of serious harmful effects from overdose. Toxicity is very low; possible effects include nausea, vomiting, and, in young girls, slight vaginal bleeding. There is no specific antidote; treatment is symptomatic.
